Mayfair, Kensington and Chelsea have long been the stomping ground of the elite -- and are now welcoming a new wave of African investors. These investors are having a considerable impact on London's property market and mainly come from Nigeria, Ghana, Congo, Gabon, Cameroon and Senegal. Nigerians are splashing out the most cash -- typically spending between $22 and $37 million on securing a property, according to luxury property agents Beauchamp Estates. Their research shows that over the past three years Africans have spent over $900 million on luxury residential property in London. High-end auction house Sotheby's says that foreign investors see London as a "safe haven" for prime property investments, and ranks the city as the second most important hub for ultra high-net-worth homes, after New York City. As well as an intelligent investment, many of the African buyers see these houses as a way of maintaining long standing cultural ties with London -- and it's here they want to send their children to school. The Nigerian Embassy in London calculates that Nigerian nationals now spend over $446 million per year on fees, tutoring and accommodation at British schools and university. Education industry experts ICEF Monitor say there were over 17,500 Nigerians studying in British universities in 2012 -- about 1,000 more than the 2009/10 academic session. "Virtually all the transactions are for end use, not rental investment, which indicates that the African buyer market in London has significant room for growth," says Gary Hersham, director at Beauchamp Estates.

Al Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula said its senior leader Ibrahim al-Rubaish was one of five people killed in an airstrike in Yemen. The group's media arm, Al-Malahem Media, said he died Monday night and described him as both a religious scholar and a combat commander. Three Yemeni defense and national security officials confirmed his death but could not establish its cause. Al-Rubaish had been detained at Guantanamo Bay, where he joined other prisoners in challenging their detention, and was later freed through Saudi Arabia's rehabilitation program for jihadist terrorists. Senator Jeff Sessions criticized that program as a failure and cited al-Rubaish in December 2009 among participants who subsequently engaged in terrorist acts. Yemen's turmoil has intensified since Houthi rebels seized Sanaa and forced President Abdu Rabu Mansour Hadi from power in January. Hadi continues to claim the presidency and is cooperating with a Saudi-led coalition against the Houthis and forces backing former President Ali Abdullah Saleh. The instability has also benefited AQAP: a senior Defense Ministry official said a prison escape earlier this month freed 270 inmates, including senior members of the group. The United States withdrew its remaining special operations personnel from Yemen last month, a move some say has made conditions easier for AQAP.

London (CNN)A Polish Prince has challenged populist British politician Nigel Farage to a duel in London's Hyde Park over his immigration policy. Farage, the leader of the UK Independence Party (UKIP), complains that Britain's membership of the European Union means it is powerless to stop a flow of foreign immigrants, many from impoverished Eastern Europe, into his "small island" nation. In a video posted on YouTube, Prince Jan Zylinski said he was fed up with discrimination against Poles living in Britain. Farage -- who is on the campaign trail ahead of Britain's general elections on May 7 -- said he did not intend to cross swords with the prince.

Hawaii's legislature on Friday passed a bill raising the minimum legal age to buy tobacco or e-cigarettes from 18 to 21, poised to make Hawaii the first state in the nation to prohibit such sales to anybody under age 21. Gov. David Ige's signature would make it law as of January 1, 2016, but it was not clear Monday whether he would sign, and a spokeswoman said he would need some time to review the bill. An Institute of Medicine report estimated that setting the minimum age at 21 nationwide would result in nearly a quarter-million fewer premature deaths and 50,000 fewer deaths from lung cancer among people born between 2000 and 2019. Under the Hawaii bill, anyone caught breaking the law would face a $10 fine for the first offense and a $50 fine or community service for a second offense.

Julian Assange, who denies the 2010 rape and molestation allegations and has not been charged, has agreed to questioning by Swedish prosecutors in London, his lawyer said. Prosecutors changed their position as some alleged crimes approach the August 2015 statute-of-limitations deadline, but must still seek British and Ecuadorian permission to interview him at the Ecuadorian Embassy, where he has stayed since June 2012 to avoid extradition to Sweden.
